summary: Project orbiteen is a serverless, browser-based 3D Earth application built with Three.js that turns NASA Earth observation data into an interactive visual experience for exploring environmental and disaster events. Users can spin an interactive 3D globe rendered with NASA Blue Marble imagery, filter categories such as wildfires, floods, earthquakes, glaciers, and agriculture, and switch between specific dates and "Live" mode. Selecting an event smoothly flies the 3D camera to the target location, triggers custom visual effects (such as fire and smoke particles, shockwaves, or storm spirals), and pairs an explanatory info card with side-by-side "Before & After" NISAR GCOV radar backscatter comparisons, 12-day radar time-lapses, MODIS optical views, and Wikipedia/Wikimedia Commons context photos.   By fetching live events from NASA EONET and loading NISAR radar and MODIS optical layers directly on the fly via NASA GIBS (WMS) without a custom backend or heavy scientific software, orbiteen makes radar surface-change insights—such as burn scars and flooding visible through clouds and smoke—fast, intuitive, and accessible to anyone.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Project orbiteen is an interactive, serverless 3D Earth web application that transforms NASA Earth observation datasets into an accessible visual explorer for environmental phenomena and natural hazards. Users spin a 3D globe rendered with NASA Blue Marble imagery, filter categories such as wildfires, floods, earthquakes, glaciers, and agriculture, and choose either a specific date or "Live" mode. When an event is selected, the camera smoothly flies to the target coordinates and triggers custom 3D visual effects (such as fire and smoke particles, shockwaves, or storm spirals), paired with an explanatory info card. Below the globe, users can inspect a side-by-side "Before & After" NISAR GCOV radar backscatter slider, a 12-day radar time-lapse animation, a MODIS optical comparison view, and real context photos from Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons.

Under the hood, the app runs completely client-side in the browser. It pulls active events from NASA EONET (alongside a curated archive of 20 major events), resolves categories and dates to the closest match, converts geographic latitude and longitude into 3D spherical rotation angles, and sends direct WMS requests to NASA GIBS on the fly to stitch radar and optical layers without a backend server.

Benefits & Intended Impact Radar satellite data is uniquely valuable because it penetrates cloud cover and wildfire smoke where optical cameras fail, yet raw radar products often require specialized software and domain expertise. orbiteen bridges this gap by turning NISAR backscatter changes (such as burn scars, flooding, and surface alterations) into intuitive visual comparisons anyone can explore in seconds. Its intended impact is educational and public-facing: helping students, educators, and curious citizens understand how radar and optical Earth observations complement each other during active and historical events.

Tools, Languages & Technologies

  • Languages & Web Stack: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+)
  • 3D Graphics & Visualization: Three.js (real-time 3D globe rendering, smooth camera flight interpolation, custom shaders, and particle systems)
  • Data & APIs: NASA EONET API, NASA GIBS (WMS) for NISAR GCOV backscatter and MODIS Terra optical layers, NASA Blue Marble imagery, Wikipedia & Wikimedia Commons APIs
  • Hardware: Standard consumer laptop/desktop hardware (no GPU cluster or server infrastructure required)

Creativity & Design Considerations Instead of presenting static charts or heavy GIS interfaces, orbiteen combines a tactile 3D globe flight with lightweight, real-time disaster shaders and synchronized "Before & After" radar/optical views. When designing the experience, we prioritized accessibility, speed, and clarity: keeping the architecture 100% serverless so it loads directly in a browser, using NISAR GCOV backscatter brightness layers rather than heavy raw interferograms for fast visual change detection, and pairing radar views with MODIS optical imagery and Wikipedia context so users can immediately grasp both the science and the real-world story behind an event.
